newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany, France bring differences on EMU into open.
newsitem.headline: Germany, France bring differences on EMU into open.

text.p: The carefully stage-managed economic relationship between Bonn and Paris is being laid open to public view, revealing fundamental differences in their approach to Europe's economic and monetary union, economists said on Tuesday.

With less than a year to go before participants in the first wave of the union are chosen, Germany and France look less able to paper over markedly different economic values and are less willing to hide the fact they disagree.
"The philosophy gap between Germany and France has become more public," said Joachim Fels, economist at Morgan Stanley in London. "Differences are coming out into the open."

Since the Maastricht Treaty was signed in 1991, Bonn and Paris have been careful to present a united front on monetary union, mindful that the financial markets would interpret any disagreement as a sign of lack commitment to the project.

Only days before the Franco-German summit on June 13, however, all that appears set to change, with the new French government willing to publicly debate EMU issues, knowing that many French voters resent the project.
France's plea for time to consider the so-called "stability pact", brainchild of German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, could be only the first hint of an increasingly public debate, economists said.

The pact, first agreed last December, lays out strict rules on government spending, but the new French government has been reluctant to give its final blessing to the scheme which some in Paris fear may prevent member governments from conducting flexible economic policies in areas such as unemployment or social security.
But for Germans, the stability pact is a way of ensuring the stability of the Euro and an asset in convincing the reluctant public it would not loose out on the disappearance of the deutschmark.
"There are fundamental differences about government intervention in the economy," said Stefan Schneider, economist at Paribas Capital Markets in Frankfurt. "France is much more interventionist."

On Tuesday, the German press went as far as to accuse France's new Socialist rulers of trying to revive what it called interventionist policies of the 1960s after Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn asked for delay in deciding whether to endorse the stability pact.
"It's not a question of protocol. The reality is that this is an attempt to mobilise monetary and financial policy to push back unemployment," the Frankfurther Allgemeine Zeitung daily said.
Analysts said that while there is little chance that Germany will allow any major changes to the stability pact, the French-German debate could flare up more intensively in other areas.

Paris, for example, is seeking to create a special council to act as a political counterweight to the European Central Bank and would like to have Europe agree to written provisions ensuring job creation will be a priority.
Both proposals have already won stern rebukes from Germany's Bundesbank which is desperate to minimise political influence on the post-euro European economy.
Analysts said the prospect of continued open debate could roil financial markets, at least in the short-term.
Fights between France and Germany would lead investors to invest more funds in Germany, considered to be the strongest economy among all possible EMU members.
That would lead to de-convergence of European bond yields and could send the mark higher against its European counterparts, hitting fragile German recovery.
